title: Mixtures and Alligation
tagline: Year 2 — Mean price, the alligation cross, and replacement problems

introduction.overview: A mixture problem combines two or more ingredients of different price, strength or concentration and asks for the mixing ratio, the mean value or the quantity of one ingredient. Alligation is a fast method for finding the ratio in which two items must be mixed to get a required mean value. A second type, replacement, removes part of a mixture and replaces it with another ingredient, repeatedly.
introduction.placementRelevance: Mixture and alligation questions are commonly asked in company aptitude rounds. The alligation cross solves in one line a problem that otherwise needs two equations.
introduction.realWorldContext: Blending tea or coffee grades, diluting a chemical solution, preparing alloys and mixing fuel grades all use these ideas.

learningObjectives: Find the mean price or strength of a mixture
Use the alligation rule to find the mixing ratio
Solve replacement problems with the (1 − x/n)ᵏ formula
Compute profit when a mixture is sold at a given price

prerequisiteKnowledge.quickRefresher: The mean (weighted average) of two items is (q₁p₁ + q₂p₂) ÷ (q₁ + q₂). Ratios can be written as parts, and concentrations as fractions.

coreDefinitions: Mean price (cost price of the mixture): the price per unit of the mixture, which lies between the two component prices.
Alligation: a rule giving the ratio in which two items are mixed: (dearer − mean) : (mean − cheaper).
Concentration: the fraction or percentage of an ingredient in a mixture.
Replacement: removing some mixture and replacing it with an equal amount of another ingredient.
Weighted average: an average where each item is weighted by its quantity.
conceptExplanation.theoreticalIntuition: The mean sits between the two prices, and it sits closer to the one that is present in the larger quantity. The ratio of quantities is therefore the inverse ratio of the distances from the mean: the farther price is present in the smaller quantity.
conceptExplanation.visualOrMentalModel: Draw the alligation cross: cheaper price on the left, dearer on the right, mean in the middle. Subtract diagonally. The result gives the ratio of cheaper : dearer quantities in the form (dearer − mean) : (mean − cheaper).

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Alligation rule
importantRulesAndFormulas.description: Works for prices, concentrations and alloy purity.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Replacement
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: Final quantity of original = Q × (1 − x/Q)ⁿ
importantRulesAndFormulas.description: Q = container volume, x = amount replaced each time, n = repetitions.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Adding a pure ingredient
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: New concentration = (old amount + x) ÷ (old total + x)

mainNarrative: For mean price, treat quantities as weights. If 3 kg of tea at ₹40 is mixed with 2 kg at ₹60, the total cost is 120 + 120 = ₹240 for 5 kg, so the mean is ₹48 per kg.

Alligation reverses the process. To get a mean of ₹24 from ₹20 and ₹30, the differences are 30 − 24 = 6 and 24 − 20 = 4, so the ratio of cheaper to dearer is 6 : 4 = 3 : 2. The cheaper item is in the larger quantity because the mean is closer to it.

Concentration problems use the same rule. A 30% and a 50% solution mixed to give 42% need (50 − 42) : (42 − 30) = 8 : 12 = 2 : 3. Water is a 0% solution and pure milk is a 100% solution, which turns dilution problems into alligation.

Replacement: if x litres are drawn out of a Q-litre vessel of pure milk and replaced by water, the milk fraction becomes (1 − x/Q). After n repetitions, the milk is Q(1 − x/Q)ⁿ. With 80 L, 20 L replaced twice: 80 × (3/4)² = 45 L milk, 35 L water.
When a seller mixes water with milk and sells at the price of pure milk, the profit percentage is (water ÷ milk) × 100. One litre of water for every 4 litres of milk gives 25% profit.

deepDiveAspects.title: Why alligation works
deepDiveAspects.content: The mean is a balance point: the cheaper quantity times its distance from the mean equals the dearer quantity times its distance. That gives the inverse proportion between quantity and distance.

deepDiveAspects.title: Repeated replacement
deepDiveAspects.content: The remaining original quantity is multiplied by the same factor (1 − x/Q) each time, so the result is a geometric decrease. Remember that the amount removed in each step is a mixture, not pure milk.

solvedExamples.title: Alligation ratio
solvedExamples.question: In what ratio must rice at ₹20 per kg be mixed with rice at ₹30 per kg to get a mixture worth ₹24 per kg?
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: The mean is closer to ₹20, so more of the cheaper rice is needed.

solvedExamples.title: Replacement
solvedExamples.question: A vessel holds 80 litres of pure milk. 20 litres are removed and replaced with water. The process is repeated once more. How much milk is left?
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: Each replacement leaves 3/4 of the milk.

solvedExamples.title: Profit on a mixture
solvedExamples.question: A trader mixes 26 kg of rice at ₹20/kg with 30 kg of rice at ₹36/kg and sells the mixture at ₹30/kg. Find his profit percentage.
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: The profit is ₹80 on a cost of ₹1,600.

shortcutMethods.title: The alligation cross

traditionalVsShortcut.traditionalMethod: Write two equations in the unknown quantities.
traditionalVsShortcut.shortcutMethod: Draw the cross: cheaper and dearer on top, mean in the middle, subtract diagonally. The two differences are the ratio.

rulesForApplication: Mean must lie between the two prices.
Replacement: multiply by (1 − x/Q) each time.
Check the ratio direction: more of the item nearer the mean.

commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Mixing up which difference goes with which item.
commonMistakes.howToAvoid: Remember: the difference with the dearer price goes with the cheaper quantity.

commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Averaging ₹20 and ₹30 as ₹25 regardless of quantity.

commonMistakes.howToAvoid: Use the cost of the mixture.

placementTips.eliminationTechnique: The mean must lie between the two component values; the ratio direction must favour the nearer one.
placementTips.questionSelectionAdvice: Replacement questions are a common difficulty step; learn the (1 − x/Q)ⁿ formula.
placementTips.recruiterInsight: Alligation is also used for averages and speed questions.
